title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:26–31)
hookLine: carrying the cross, he stops to comfort weeping women

lines: SIMON OF CYRENE, PULLED FROM THE ROAD.
cards: A man is coming into the city from the countryside, minding his own business. His name is Simon, from Cyrene, in North Africa.

Suddenly soldiers grab him and put a wooden beam on his shoulders, and he's walking behind a condemned man he's never met. That's how Luke starts the road to the cross: with a stranger forced to help.

Behind them follows a great crowd, and among them, women, beating their breasts and wailing, the way people mourned the dead. And Jesus, who has barely spoken since the courtyard, stops and turns to them.

teach.b: In the King James words: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children."
Beaten through the night, mocked by soldiers, walking to his own execution, he has every reason to be wrapped up in his own pain.

And he turns to the people grieving for him and thinks about them. He looks ahead to days of suffering coming for that city, when people will call the childless blessed and ask the mountains to fall on them.
Then a proverb, hard to translate and harder to pin down: "For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in the dry?"

teach.h: WEEP FOR YOURSELVES AND YOUR CHILDREN.
teach.b: Green wood is hard to burn; dry wood catches at once. One common reading: if this is what's done to an innocent man now, think how much worse it will be when the times are dry.

teach.h: THE GREEN TREE AND THE DRY.
teach.b: Scholars debate who the they is and exactly what's meant; the saying doesn't explain itself.

teach.h: DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM, WEEP NOT FOR ME.
teach.b: Many connect his warning to the Roman siege of Jerusalem a generation later. Only Luke tells this scene: women openly mourning him on the road, and Jesus stopping to speak to them.
Later it became part of the Stations of the Cross, the devotion where Christians walk the way to Calvary in fourteen stops; Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem is the eighth.
On the worst day of his life, he still turns toward someone else's grief.

how: Many Christians, especially Catholics and Anglicans, pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, stopping at the eighth station to remember Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

games.q: you're walking to your execution, exhausted. women in the crowd are weeping for you. what do you do?
o: turn and tell them to weep for themselves and their children.
games.why: "daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." even now, he's thinking about them.

practice: Name honestly what's hard for you right now, and let it be real.

Then, without pushing it away, think of one person near you who is also carrying something, a friend after a breakup, a coworker with a sick parent, a lonely neighbor, and picture one small comfort you could offer from inside your own hard week.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Calvary. The place of the cross that Jesus walked toward while stopping to speak to the weeping daughters of Jerusalem, now the eighth stop of the Stations of the Cross.

orig.note: Greek: daughters of Jerusalem. a biblical way of addressing the women of the city, found also in the Song of Songs.

carryVoice: Your line: weep not for me. Spoken by a man with every reason to think only of himself. Day five hundred eighty-five, done.
